newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Netanyahu insists deals won't stop budget cuts.
newsitem.headline: Netanyahu insists deals won't stop budget cuts.

text.p: Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu vowed in an interview to slash Israel's budget deficit as promised and still meet the deals he made with coalition partners to defuse political crises.

"We'll invest a lot of money now in education, especially in the developing towns -- without breaking out of the framework of the budget," he told the newspaper Yedioth Ahronoth in the interview published on Friday.

Netanyahu has resolved disputes with Foreign Minister David Levy's Gesher faction and the Yisrael ba-Aliya immigrant party by signing agreements which newspapers this week said would cost up to three billion shekels ($845 million).

Asked about estimates the deal with Levy would cost a billion shekels, Netanyahu, who heads the rightist Likud party, told Yedioth Ahronoth: "Nonsense. The agreement is only an expression of a general intention.
"Everything in it will be discussed only in the framework of the budget," said Netanyahu, whose deal outlined Levy's diplomatic and peacemaking duties along with promises to increase social spending.

Levy's Gesher faction -- built on support for Israel's poorer citizens with origins in Arab countries -- had threatened to bolt from the splintered coalition, charging Netanyahu had violated promises and usurped Levy's responsibilities.
The prime minister -- who has promised economic reforms including privatisation and deregulation -- insisted there was no contradiction between a free market and doing right by those who needed help.

"A release of the economy from its chains is no simple act. Interested elements want the chains to remain, because they enjoy their protection. Economic freedom frightens them, places question marks on the existing order, pushes towards competition. I am committed to competition," he said.

Treasury officials have recommended a four billion shekel budget cut in 1998 to reduce inflationary pressure and revive sustainable growth. A large budget deficit in June prompted the Bank of Israel to call for immediate spending cuts.
Deficit targets set by law are 2.8 percent of GDP this year, 2.4 percent in 1998 and 1.2 percent within five years.
